displayQuote: Always be sincere, even if you don't mean it

meta.title: Who really said "Always be sincere, even if you don't mean it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Harry Truman never said it. The line is a 1950s American gag: first documented in a 1951 comic strip, later credited to Edgar Bergen's dummy Mortimer Snerd.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Always be sincere, even if you don't mean it'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Truman. Earliest print: a 1951 'Modest Maidens' comic strip; the exact wording turns up in 1960 credited to Mortimer Snerd. The Truman credit is disputed.

answer.label: Not Harry S. Truman — a 1950s American gag
answer.authorName: Unknown — an anonymous American gag line
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · earliest documented 23 July 1951, in a newspaper comic strip
answer.sourceLine: The line is an anonymous American joke of the early 1950s. Its earliest documented appearance is a “Modest Maidens” comic strip of 23 July 1951, and from April 1954 newspapers printed it as the property of Mortimer Snerd, Edgar Bergen’s ventriloquist dummy. Truman’s name attached to it decades later, in a reference book that supplied no citation.

source.excerpt: Personal relationships must be rooted in a sincerity which can be trusted. Have you ever heard Mortimer Snerd’s definition of sincerity? Well, Mortimer Snerd said, “Always be sincere, even if you don’t mean it.”
trail: 23 July 1951 — the earliest citation on record is not a president but a newspaper cartoon. The Corpus Christi Times ran a “Modest Maidens” strip by Jay Alan (pen name of J. Alan Klein) carrying “My dear, there’s nothing like being sincere, whether you mean it or not!” Barry Popik transcribes it from page 15 ↗.

1954 — the gag attaches itself to a ventriloquist’s dummy. The San Diego Union of 14 April and the Chicago Daily Tribune of 12 December both print it as Mortimer Snerd’s: “Always be sincere, whether you mean it or not.” Both columns are transcribed in Popik’s entry ↗. Snerd was the slow-witted second dummy of Edgar Bergen ↗.

1960 — the modern wording appears verbatim, still credited to Snerd, in a West Virginia University Engineering Experiment Station Bulletin: “Always be sincere, even if you don’t mean it.” By 1963 the Rev. Ross Coggins is quoting it in a paper read at a Texas church workshop, and by 1972 Earl Wilson is calling it fortune-cookie wisdom. All three are dated in the trail ↗.

1992, then 2006 — The Oxford Dictionary of Quotations credits Truman with no citation attached; Ralph Keyes’s The Quote Verifier replies that it is not something the president is known to have said, nor was likely to have said. Wikiquote files it under Disputed ↗.
source.excerptNote: Engineering Experiment Station Bulletin, West Virginia University, issues 57–58 (1960), p. 24, as transcribed by Barry Popik. It is the earliest citation in his trail to carry the wording exactly as it circulates today — and it credits a ventriloquist’s dummy, not a president.

source.rightsNote: No identifiable authored work is the origin of this wording. The earliest documented appearance is a 1951 newspaper comic strip carrying a variant, and the exact modern sentence surfaces in 1960 credited to a comedy character — both well after the 1931 United States public-domain cut-off, and neither established as the source. Because the coiner and the originating work are both unknown, quotle.info asserts no copyright status for this sentence.

author.name: Edgar Bergen
author.heading: The closest thing to an author
author.bio: Bergen (16 February 1903 – 30 September 1978) was the American ventriloquist whose dummies — the wisecracking Charlie McCarthy and the slow-witted Mortimer Snerd — became national radio stars on a medium where nobody could see the trick. From April 1954 onward American joke columns printed the sincerity gag as Snerd’s line, and a 1960 university bulletin still called it “Mortimer Snerd’s definition of sincerity” — the earliest appearance of the wording exactly as it circulates today. That does not make Bergen the coiner: a variant was already in print in July 1951 with no connection to him, and mid-century gag columns routinely hung stray jokes on whichever comic character was popular. No source documents who wrote it.

misattribution.heading: Three names, none of them the author
misattribution.intro: This line has been carried by a president, a ventriloquist’s dummy and a pair of British cabaret comedians. The dated record puts one of them years after the line was already in American print, treats another as a vehicle rather than an author, and gives the third no support at all.

items.why: The Oxford Dictionary of Quotations attributed the line to Truman without a citation, and Ralph Keyes’s The Quote Verifier (2006, p. 224) answered that it is “not something the president is known to have said or is likely to have said.” Not one of the newspaper or book citations running from July 1951 to October 1972 mentions Truman at all. Popik transcribes both the citations and the Keyes entry ↗.

From April 1954 the gag ran in newspaper joke columns as Snerd’s — “Always be sincere, whether you mean it or not” — and a 1960 West Virginia University bulletin still introduced it as “Mortimer Snerd’s definition of sincerity.” But a variant was already in print in July 1951 in a comic strip with no connection to Bergen, and gag columns of the period routinely hung stray jokes on whichever comic character was popular. The 1951, 1954 and 1960 citations, side by side ↗.

Earl Wilson credited the line to Michael Flanders in the Milwaukee Sentinel of 1 December 1959, and it is still repeated as the duo’s. But their revue At the Drop of a Hat opened on 31 December 1956 — after the American citations of 1951 and 1954. Wikipedia dates the revue’s opening night ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who wrote it. It is an anonymous American gag of the early 1950s that passed through a comic strip, a ventriloquist’s dummy, a droodle column and a fortune cookie before a reference book handed it to a president. Barry Popik’s dated citation trail, 1951 to 1972 ↗.

context.heading: A joke about a joke
lead: The saying is a paradox with a punchline: sincerity is the one quality that cannot survive being performed, so an instruction to perform it is funny by construction. That is exactly the register the earliest citations sit in — a flirtatious newspaper cartoon, a ventriloquist’s dummy, Roger Price’s Droodles column, and finally, by 1972, a fortune cookie. It was never advice. It was a gag about the people who give advice.

Which is why the Truman credit is so odd, and so sticky. Truman’s public reputation was blunt plain-speaking, so a cynical aside about faking sincerity reads, to a modern ear, like something he might have muttered on the way out of a room. That plausibility is the whole mechanism: nobody checked, because it sounded like him.
context.detailsSummary: How a dummy’s line became a president’s
detailsBody: The wording drifts across Popik’s citations. The 1951 strip has “there’s nothing like being sincere, whether you mean it or not.” By April 1954 it has compressed to “Always be sincere, whether you mean it or not.” The even if phrasing is already in print by February 1959 — the Salt Lake Tribune runs “All lists of personality tips include ‘be sincere.’ Even if you don’t mean it” — and the sentence reaches its modern shape in the 1960 West Virginia University bulletin. That is the shape that stuck.

The Truman credit enters the reference literature with The Oxford Dictionary of Quotations in 1992, with no citation attached — which is precisely what Wikiquote notes about it. Ralph Keyes flagged the problem in The Quote Verifier in 2006. Quote aggregators have gone on printing it under Truman’s name ever since.

The same joke has a better-known sibling: the line about faking sincerity being the secret of success, routinely pinned on Groucho Marx or Samuel Goldwyn. Quote Investigator finds no substantive evidence for either, and traces the remark no earlier than a 1962 Leonard Lyons column in which Celeste Holm relayed an unnamed actor’s version about faking honesty. Quote Investigator on the fake-honesty line ↗.
context.pull: It was never advice. It was a gag about the people who give advice.

sourcesVerified.claim: Popik states the saying is often credited to Harry S. Truman (1884-1972) but there is no evidence he said it, and the earliest citations do not credit Truman.

Popik's earliest citation is 23 July 1951, Corpus Christi (TX) Times, 'Modest Maidens' comic strip by Jay Alan (pen name of J. Alan Klein), pg. 15 col. 2: 'My dear, there's nothing like being sincere, whether you mean it or not!'

Popik transcribes the 14 April 1954 San Diego Union ('For Comedians' by Donald Freeman, pg. A10) and the 12 December 1954 Chicago Daily Tribune ('Radio-TV Gag Bag', pg. Q45) both crediting Mortimer Snerd with 'Always be sincere, whether you mean it or not.'

Popik transcribes Engineering Experiment Station Bulletin, West Virginia University, issues 57-58, 1960, pg. 24: 'Have you ever heard Mortimer Snerd's definition of sincerity? Well, Mortimer Snerd said, "Always be sincere, even if you don't mean it."' — the exact modern wording.

Popik transcribes 14 February 1959, Salt Lake Tribune, pg. 14 col. 2: 'All lists of personality tips include "be sincere." Even if you don't mean it.' — the 'even if' phrasing in print a year before the 1960 bulletin.

Popik transcribes the 1 December 1959 Milwaukee Sentinel Earl Wilson column crediting Flanders with 'Always be sincere whether you mean it or not', and the 30 October 1972 Greensboro Record Earl Wilson column calling 'Be sincere even if you don't mean it' fortune-cookie wisdom.

Popik quotes Ralph Keyes, The Quote Verifier (St. Martin's Press, 2006), p. 224: 'The Oxford Dictionary of Quotations credits Truman with "Always be sincere, even if you don't mean it," which is not something the president is known to have said or is likely to have said.'
Popik transcribes the 13 March 1963 Big Spring (TX) Herald report of Rev. Ross Coggins using the line, and Calvin Miller's Once Upon a Tree (1967), p. 40, attributing it to 'some wag'.

Wikiquote lists 'Always be sincere, even if you don't mean it' under its Disputed section for Harry S. Truman, noting it was attributed without citation in The Oxford Dictionary of Quotations (1992) by Angela Partington and disputed in Ralph Keyes's The Quote Verifier (2006), p. 224. It gives Truman's dates as May 8, 1884 – December 26, 1972.

Wikipedia gives Edgar Bergen's dates as February 16, 1903 – September 30, 1978, describes him as an American ventriloquist and radio performer, and identifies Mortimer Snerd as his slow-witted character alongside Charlie McCarthy.
Wikipedia states that in December 1956 Flanders and Swann hired the New Lindsey Theatre, Notting Hill, for their revue At the Drop of a Hat, which opened on New Year's Eve (31 December 1956).
The Internet Archive item is Ralph Keyes, The Quote Verifier: Who Said What, Where, and When, St. Martin's Press, 2006, 422 pages, available as an access-restricted borrowable scan.

Quote Investigator finds no substantive evidence ascribing the fake-sincerity/honesty remark to Groucho Marx or Samuel Goldwyn, and traces it no earlier than a 1962 Leonard Lyons column in which Celeste Holm relayed an unnamed actor's version about faking honesty; the coiner remains anonymous.
